To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the storage volume of hydrate-based secondary fluids can be reduced by up to 75 % when vapor compression is used.
the storage capacity of a gas hydrate secondary refrigeration system can be increased by adding vapor compression and that this increase is greater for the mixed hydrate than for the single hydrate.

the use of vapor compression to separate vapor from hydrate slurry in secondary refrigeration systems can reduce the required storage volume by 75% and can be applied to both pure carbon dioxide hydrates and to mixed hydrate of TBPB plus carbon dioxide.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the management of vapor release in gas hydrate secondary refrigeration processes.
the design and optimization of the storage system of a gas hydrate slurry-based refrigeration system.
the management of gas vapor released during hydrate melting and the design of storage systems to use hydrates as secondary refrigerants in cold storage applications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the vapor release phenomenon should be taken into account in the design of the secondary refrigeration processes involving gas hydrates.
the storage of hydrates in cold rooms for refrigeration and cold storage applications is feasible and that the use of vapor compression can reduce storage volume significantly.

the storage volume of the system is a function of the heat transfer area of the heat exchangers and the pressure of the storage tank, and the use of vapor compression can significantly reduce the required storage volume.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the storage volume required for hydrate slurry is significantly lower than that required for a pure refrigerant, and this advantage increases with the number of compression stages.

vapor release in hydrate slurries can be used to reduce the volume of the storage system and, consequently, the cost of the process, provided that the vapor is properly separated and used in a vapor compression cycle.

, for an energy density of 1.5 MJ/kg of storage volume, the storage volume of a system using gas hydrate slurtries as secondary fluid can be 75% less than that required for a system using a secondary fluid with the same energy density, if vapor compression is added to the process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the design of the cold storage system must be adapted to the specificities of gas hydrate slurry as a secondary refrigerant.
, when used as a secondary refrigerant in cold storage and refrigerating applications, the vapor release from hydrates should be taken into account.
the use of vapor compression in combination with hydrate slurry as a secondary refrigerant offers an energy-efficient and environmentally friendly solution for cold storage.
